statements.quote: We developed a customized interface that was divided into two sections. The left section was dedicated to task description and idea submission, which was identical for the two conditions, and the right section was designated for either an LLM or search engine.
statements.locator: p. 9, Section 4 (Experimental Setup); description of study materials, with no code-release statement.

statements.quote: For the LLM, we employed OpenAI’s Chat Completion API and the GPT-3.5-turbo model to generate responses to user prompts.
statements.locator: p. 9, Section 4; footnote 3 links to vendor documentation.
p. 9, footnote 3; vendor documentation, not study code or data.

statements.quote: For the Search Engine tool, we utilized Google’s Custom Search JSON API to generate results for search queries.
statements.locator: p. 10, Section 4; footnote 4 links to vendor documentation.
p. 10, footnote 4; vendor documentation, not study code or data.

statements.quote: Figures 2 and 3 display screenshots of the interface for each tool.
statements.locator: p. 10, Section 4; Figures 2-3 are in the PDF.

statements.quote: We monitored participants’ fine-grained behavior on the interface. In the LLM condition, we recorded all user prompts and the corresponding responses. In the Search Engine condition, we tracked each query, clicks on results, and the content of visited websites. We also recorded the duration of each participant’s stay on the interface. We required participants to type in their MTurk ID before starting the task so that we could match the collected behavior data with their submissions.
statements.locator: p. 11, Section 4; collection/linkage of participant data, with no availability statement.

statements.quote: Before the task, participants underwent a training task to familiarize them with the tool’s functionalities, which showed several examples of how users could interact with the tool; these examples were not relevant to idea generation. To proceed to the task page, participants in the LLM condition were required to send at least one message to ChatGPT, and participants in the Search Engine condition were required to input at least one query. The interface used in the training task closely resembled that assigned to the specific condition.
statements.locator: p. 11, Section 4; training materials described, with no separate materials link.

statements.quote: After participants completed the tasks, we asked them to fill out a questionnaire with attention checks and requests for relevant information. Ten participants who failed attention checks were removed. Our final sample comprised 90 participants, with 45 for each tool. We collected their level of enjoyment while working on the task, experience with LLM or search engines, knowledge of product design, and demographic information (e.g., age, gender, level of education).
statements.locator: p. 11, Section 4; questionnaire data described, with no availability statement.

statements.quote: Specifically, we employed ChatGPT (the GPT-3.5-turbo model) for preprocessing, using the following prompt: “A café has recently collected numerous novel ideas about coffee mugs. However, the writing styles used in these ideas vary. Please summarize each idea in no more than 10 words. I will provide you with all the ideas and their corresponding numbers. Please conduct the summarization one by one. The following are the collected ideas: …”
statements.locator: pp. 12-13, Section 5.1 (Preprocessing); the summarization prompt is printed in the paper.

statements.quote: For instance, an initial submission, such as “Temperature-controlled mug: a mug that automatically adjusts the temperature of your drink to your desired level and keeps it hot for longer periods” was summarized as “Temperature-controlled mugs to adjust and maintain desired heat.” To ensure the quality of a summary, two postgraduate students were recruited to verify if it matched the initial texts. When it was invalid, we reran the prompt until we obtained a valid summary. The resulting summarized text was utilized for scoring and analysis purposes.
statements.locator: p. 13, Section 5.1; one illustrative original idea and its summary, not an identified participant dataset.

statements.quote: We conduct a set of mediation analyses to investigate whether the impacts of using ChatGPT on ideation outcomes were mediated by the process variables. Appendix A shows the detailed results.
statements.locator: p. 20, Section 6.2.1; Appendix A is included on pp. 33-37.
p. 33; heading of the in-PDF appendix, Tables A1-A5 on pp. 33-37.

notes:
Read the entire 77,469-character markdown conversion, including references and Appendix A (all 37 PDF pages). Checked relevant quotations and locators against PyMuPDF text, inspected all PDF hyperlinks, and confirmed that the PDF contains no embedded files. Quotations preserve source wording and punctuation; PDF line breaks are normalized to spaces.

The source is the undated SSRN working paper held in retrieval.json. No newer version is listed there. The first author is Jiexin Zheng; the second author's name in the PDF is Ka Chau Wong. S1 is the only randomized study in forms/c170.json.

No data-availability, code-availability, preregistration, repository, external supplementary-file, or available-on-request statement was found. The form's data_url and code_url are both empty. The statements above record the paper's own URL, in-paper materials and participant-data collection descriptions, vendor documentation footnotes, and the in-PDF appendix reference; none promises public study data. Appendix A (pp. 33-37) contains only aggregate mediation tables. Interface screenshots, a summarization prompt, and one illustrative idea/summary are printed in the paper; they do not constitute a participant-linked text dataset.

No deposit belonging to c170 was identified in the named repository searches, so no deposit file list, data rows, columns, or license could be verified. Unrelated search hits, vendor documentation, and the article itself are not counted as deposits. The repository-specific file-list endpoints are inapplicable because no relevant node, dataset DOI, or record ID was found. No GitHub repository is named in the paper and no GitHub API request was made.

All HTTP requests used Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no email or personal identifier. Searches used the distinctive title phrase and the shorter phrase 'Ideation for Product Innovation', plus the first author's name. Where unquoted name searches were too broad, exact-name searches in both name orders were used. OSF's specified endpoint only filters titles; the author-name query does not exhaust contributor-linked projects. Initial Zenodo size=100 requests returned HTTP 400, so searches were retried with the permitted anonymous size=25. Identical repeated requests are consolidated in the search log.

Medium confidence refers to the finding that no public data were located, not proof that no deposit exists. All four named repository APIs ultimately answered successfully, but the SSRN landing page was blocked by a bot check. A bot check is not evidence of an account/approval restriction on an identified data deposit; therefore status is none_found rather than restricted. The paper does not say data are available on request, so on_request is not supported.

No public data can currently resolve final.open_items: the inconsistent novelty difference and outcome labels, corrected divergence summaries, arm SDs and unadjusted arm-difference SEs, allocation/exclusion counts, rater counts and evaluated idea set, actual divergence sample and comparison rule, or mediation-model sample sizes. Participant-level scores with arm labels, or idea-level scores/texts with participant IDs and arm labels plus exclusion/analysis flags, would be needed to recover those quantities; no such columns were read. No diversity measure can be reconstructed from the single illustrative idea.
